subject: english-language

moments.title: Sacks's UCLA lectures
moments.who: Harvey Sacks, Emanuel Schegloff, Gail Jefferson
moments.body: 1960s: Harvey Sacks (1935-1975) gives lectures at UCLA on conversation. He records telephone calls (including a suicide hotline) and analyses them in extraordinary detail. The lectures (published posthumously, 1992) are foundational to conversation analysis (CA).
moments.takeaway: Sacks died young (car accident, 1975). Schegloff and Jefferson carried the project forward.

moments.title: A Simplest Systematics
moments.body: 1974: 'A Simplest Systematics for the Organization of Turn-Taking for Conversation' published in Language. The paper analyses how speakers manage turn-taking — without explicit instructions or central coordination. Turn-construction units, transition-relevance places, and a set of rules.
moments.takeaway: The paper is one of the most-cited in linguistics. CA's combination of close empirical observation and systematic analysis is hard to replicate.

moments.title: Institutional and cross-cultural CA
moments.body: CA extends to medical encounters (doctor-patient), courtroom talk, news interviews, classrooms. Cross-cultural CA examines how conversational structures vary across languages. Modern multimodal CA includes gaze, gesture and embodiment.
moments.takeaway: CA is now widely used in applied linguistics, sociology, communication studies. The Conversation Analytic Roundtable and biennial conferences sustain the field.

now.title: Talk as ordered
now.body: Conversation analysis has shown that what looks like chaotic talk is highly organised. Modern CA continues to extend to new domains — telemedicine, online video chat, AI assistants. The methods are continuous: detailed transcription, sequence analysis, careful description.
now.open_questions: What does CA explain? Critics argue it describes patterns without explaining them; defenders argue description at this level is itself explanation of a sort.

reflection: A series of UCLA lectures founded the field that takes everyday conversation seriously as an organised social activity. CA's methodological rigour and empirical depth have made it one of the most distinctive 20th-century contributions to language study.
